IntroHero.headline.note: The introduction's headline (the page's first words for a new visitor). A title: no period.

IntroHero.lede.message: $t(common:product.name) emulates the hardware, not an operating system. Boot generic, UEFI-ready ARM Linux images, unmodified, with their own kernels, in your browser. Run complete systems, with graphics acceleration, network connectivity, shared folders, and even USB support.

IntroMade.lede.message: $t(common:product.name) was created by a single individual with copious amounts of AI assistance, to the point that the project's informal codename was “slopulator”. That was almost its final name, but I figured that I had put enough of my own thinking into achieving a high quality result that it could no longer be considered sloppy. Here are some conclusions.

IntroMade.code.words.message: Effectively all of the code was written by Claude Opus 5.5, with a minority of it by Claude Fable 5.2. Some of the UI/UX design and some copy adjustments were made by human hand.
IntroMade.code.words.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): which AI models wrote the code. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 are models' names: don't translate.

IntroMade.cost.words.message: Two months of a Claude Max subscription, almost fully utilized. At API prices, the same usage would have cost upwards of $5000.

IntroMade.time.words.message: I estimate that getting this project to this level without AI assistance would have taken me no less than three years of full-time work - and that's as someone with 10+ years of systems programming experience.
IntroMade.time.words.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): the author's estimate of the work without AI.

IntroMade.knew.words.message: I was already conceptually aware of how a compiler works, what a JIT is, what Mesa is, what WebGPU is, and so on, but I had no hands-on experience building anything like this (not counting the compilers course in university).
IntroMade.knew.words.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): what the author knew beforehand. JIT, Mesa and WebGPU are terms and names.

IntroMade.learned.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): title of a part. No period.

IntroMade.learned.words.message: I learned a lot building the project this way, but it all feels relatively superficial. I'm sure I'd have learned much more if I had built it all by hand, but I'm also sure I wouldn't have scratched even 10% of the surface I scratched here: I would have gotten tired, and I would have had no time to explore as many options. So one can say the experience I gained is broader, even if it isn't as deep.
IntroMade.learned.words.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): what the author learned, and its limits.

IntroMade.thanks.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): heading of the acknowledgement of the open-source projects. No period.

IntroMade.thanks.words.message: I am fully aware that this is only possible in the first place because so many of the related projects are open source, have been for years, and are part of the training sets of all the AI models used. That was, undeniably, a lot of human effort, given away for free.
IntroMade.thanks.words.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): the acknowledgement that open-source projects, in the AI models' training data, made the project possible.

IntroMade.why.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): heading over a numbered list of reasons. No period.

IntroMade.why.llm.message: To find out if frontier LLMs can build something that exceeds prior art in this field. They clearly did, and both the feature set and the achieved performance levels even beat other nascent AI-assisted projects, like unkernel.
IntroMade.why.llm.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): a reason. LLM: large language model, the term of the trade.

IntroMade.why.browser.message: To showcase just how much is possible in a browser (effectively, a large portion of QEMU's feature set).
IntroMade.why.browser.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): a reason. QEMU is a program's name (the machine emulator).

IntroMade.why.upstream.message: To incentivize further development and performance optimization of technology like WebAssembly, or Mesa's virgl and Venus.
IntroMade.why.upstream.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): a reason. WebAssembly, Mesa, virgl and Venus are names.

IntroMade.why.web.message: And to showcase just how well optimized modern websites are: an entire OS and a browser will boot in here, and the slowest part will still be waiting for everything that appears around the player on a YouTube video page!
IntroMade.why.web.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person (one person made the project with AI agents): the last reason, a joke said with sarcasm: “carefully optimized” means the opposite. Keep the dry tone; the exclamation mark is the author's, and ironic.

IntroMade.close.work.message: I am being pushed to use AI so much at work that I figured that I almost had an obligation to also build something more to my taste, rather than just what the company wants, using this rather resource-intensive newfangled “AI” thing. I definitely like to use it more for my personal ideas than for work; it really excites the “curious builder” part of my brain, the one that got me into computers in the first place, while completely breaking the heart and mind of the engineer that I am.
IntroMade.close.work.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person and their own words (one person made the project with AI agents): the first of three closing paragraphs, under the list of reasons. The author's own words: keep their expressions.

IntroMade.close.friends.message: This project will not be seen in a good light by some of my friends, which is understandable and even commendable; a large part of me still finds much of all this quite objectionable too. It's extremely exciting, extremely powerful, and extremely negative as well (in so many directions), and before long we'll know whether it led us to freedom and light, or capture and darkness.
IntroMade.close.friends.note: The introduction's section “How it was made”, in the author's own first person and their own words (one person made the project with AI agents): the second closing paragraph. <i> marks words in italics. The author's own words: keep their expressions.

IntroMade.close.hurry.message: Don't worry: I get the feeling that this situation is more temporary than most things on Earth, and I suspect that, five years from now, most people won't be able to build slopulators like this, for one reason or another. Let's hurry up and value the progress of technology before it values us back.

IntroCompare.leads.syscalls.words.message: unkernel's kernel is WebAssembly itself, so a system call is a function call. WebVM has no guest kernel: its engine answers Linux system calls itself. Here a system call is an exception the emulated processor takes, handled by a kernel that is emulated too, as on real hardware, and that costs more.

IntroTranslate.sum.look.message: A load in a loop. The WebAssembly looks the address up in the TLB inline and reads the byte itself. The folded slow path is taken only when the page isn't in the TLB. The branch at the end compares the numbers directly, and the flags are only stored for whoever reads them later.
IntroTranslate.sum.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Summing bytes”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.move.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.move.look.message: Two pair loads and a pair store through one pointer. The JIT checks the TLB once for the whole group, so the accesses after the first are plain WebAssembly loads and stores, and the group shares one slow path.
IntroTranslate.move.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Moving a point”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.collatz.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.collatz.look.message: No memory at all: arithmetic, a conditional select, and a branch. The guest's registers live in WebAssembly locals, which V8 keeps in your processor's registers. The compare writes no flags. The branch after it compares the numbers itself.
IntroTranslate.collatz.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Collatz steps”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.total.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.total.look.message: Floating-point code. The addition is one WebAssembly f64.add. The lines around it check that your processor's answer is the one an ARM processor would give: the rounding mode is the default, and no operand or result is a NaN, an infinity, or a denormal. Otherwise the slow path computes it in software.
IntroTranslate.total.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Adding floats”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.why.sig.message: One WebAssembly function per block of guest code. It is given where the emulated processor's state is in memory and how many instructions it may run, and it returns how many it ran. This capture counts instructions, as our tests do. In the page, compiled code polls a flag instead.
IntroTranslate.why.sig.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: over the function's first line.

IntroTranslate.why.pc.message: The guest's program counter, read from the processor's state.
IntroTranslate.why.pc.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the three lines that load the program counter.

IntroTranslate.why.regs.message: The guest registers this block uses ({{regs}}) are copied from the processor's state in memory into locals. The block works on the copies, and V8 keeps locals in your processor's registers.
IntroTranslate.why.regs.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that load guest registers. {{regs}} is a list of register names like “x0, x1, x8”.

IntroTranslate.why.loop.message: The block branches back to its own start, so here it is a loop. A turn of the guest's loop never leaves this function.
IntroTranslate.why.loop.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the “loop” line.

IntroTranslate.why.tlb.message: A memory access. The guest's address has to become a place in WebAssembly's memory, so first comes a question: is its page in the emulated TLB? The address picks an entry, and one comparison checks that the entry is this page's.
IntroTranslate.why.tlb.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines of a load or store that check the software TLB. TLB is the term of the trade (translation lookaside buffer): keep it.

IntroTranslate.why.hit.message: It is. The entry also holds where the page is, so one addition gives the place, and the access itself is a single load or store.
IntroTranslate.why.hit.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: after the TLB check, before the fast path. Follows the note that asks whether the page is in the TLB.

IntroTranslate.why.miss.message: It isn't. The registers that changed go back to the processor's state, and a helper in the emulator's core does the access the long way: through the guest's page tables, to a device, or to a fault. Then the registers are read again.
IntroTranslate.why.miss.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: at the start of the slow path taken when the TLB check fails.

IntroTranslate.why.flags.message: The condition flags N, Z, C, and V are packed into one word of the processor's state. The compiler stores them only where something later may still read them.
IntroTranslate.why.flags.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that compute and store the guest's condition flags.

IntroTranslate.why.again.message: The branch to the block's own start, taken inside this function while the count of instructions allows.
IntroTranslate.why.again.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that jump back to the loop's start.

IntroTranslate.why.back.message: Leaving the block. The registers that changed ({{regs}}) are written back to the processor's state.
IntroTranslate.why.back.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that store guest registers. {{regs}} is a list of register names like “x0, x1, x8”.

IntroTranslate.why.pcBack.message: The program counter is written back: where the guest goes next.
IntroTranslate.why.pcBack.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that store the program counter.

IntroTranslate.why.chain.message: The next block. Its entry in the cache of compiled blocks is checked (is it the code for that address, may it still run), and if so it is entered with a tail call. Compiled blocks follow one another without returning to the emulator.
IntroTranslate.why.chain.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the lines that look up and call the next compiled block.

IntroTranslate.why.ret.message: Otherwise, back to the emulator's dispatcher with the count of instructions run.
IntroTranslate.why.ret.note: A note between the lines of the “Compiled” pane (WebAssembly) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know WebAssembly: before the function's last return.

IntroTranslate.why.hostEntry.x64.message: V8's own preamble, from no line of the WebAssembly: the function's stack frame, a check that the stack has room, and the address where WebAssembly's memory starts, kept in a register for every access below.
IntroTranslate.why.hostEntry.x64.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: over the first lines, on x86-64. V8 is the browser's JavaScript and WebAssembly engine.

IntroTranslate.why.hostEntry.arm64.message: V8's own preamble, from no line of the WebAssembly: the function's stack frame, a check that the stack has room, and the address where WebAssembly's memory starts, with its size, kept in registers for every access below.
IntroTranslate.why.hostEntry.arm64.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: over the first lines, on AArch64. V8 is the browser's JavaScript and WebAssembly engine.

IntroTranslate.why.hostRegs.x64.message: The guest's registers, read from the processor's state: the memory's start, plus the state's place in it, plus the register's offset. No access here has a bounds check. On x86-64, V8 reserves address space past the end of the memory, so an access outside it faults in your processor instead of being compared first.
IntroTranslate.why.hostRegs.x64.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the loads of guest registers, on x86-64. Explains why there are no bounds checks.

IntroTranslate.why.hostRegs.arm64.message: The guest's registers, read from the processor's state: the memory's start, plus the state's place in it, plus the register's offset. V8 leaves these loads unchecked in this build. It checks the stores further down.
IntroTranslate.why.hostRegs.arm64.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the loads of guest registers, on AArch64.

IntroTranslate.why.hostLoop.message: V8's own check at every turn of a loop: it reads a flag, so that the browser can interrupt code that runs for long.
IntroTranslate.why.hostLoop.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the two instructions V8 adds at a loop's head.

IntroTranslate.why.hostTlb.message: The TLB check, as in the WebAssembly beside it: shift and mask the address to pick the entry, compare, and branch away to the slow path if the entry isn't this page's.
IntroTranslate.why.hostTlb.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the machine code of a TLB check.

IntroTranslate.why.hostGray.message: Not lit, because V8 names a line of WebAssembly only for loads, stores, and calls. These are the sums, compares, and condition flags of the instructions around them, done in your processor's registers.
IntroTranslate.why.hostGray.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before a run of lines that no guest instruction lights up.

IntroTranslate.why.hostBounds.message: A bounds check: three instructions that compare the address with the memory's size before a store. This code was captured on Linux, where V8 on AArch64 can't rely on a fault for an access outside the memory, so it checks every store. Chrome on a Mac leaves these out, as x86-64 does.
IntroTranslate.why.hostBounds.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the first bounds check, on AArch64 only.

IntroTranslate.why.hostExit.message: Leaving the block: the changed registers and the program counter are stored back into the processor's state.
IntroTranslate.why.hostExit.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the stores that end the block.

IntroTranslate.why.hostChain.message: The jump into the next block: the lookup in the cache of compiled blocks, then V8's code for the tail call, with its own checks that the table's entry exists and has this function's type.
IntroTranslate.why.hostChain.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the machine code that looks up and jumps to the next block.

IntroTranslate.why.hostRare.message: From here on, the rare paths, placed after the code that normally runs: the calls into V8 when one of its checks above fails, and the slow path's call into the emulator's core.
IntroTranslate.why.hostRare.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: where the out-of-line code starts.

IntroTranslate.why.hostSlow.message: The slow path: registers saved, the core's helper called for the access that missed the TLB, registers restored, and back into the block.
IntroTranslate.why.hostSlow.note: A note between the lines of the “What your processor runs” pane (machine code) in the introduction's code viewer, in plain words for a reader who doesn't know assembly: before the machine code of the slow path's helper call.

IntroTranslate.honest.message: Nothing here is drawn by hand. The guest's code ran in $t(common:product.name), and these are its micro-ops and the WebAssembly it emitted, printed by wasm-tools. The machine code is what {{compiler}} made of that function. V8 says which line a load, a store, or a call came from, so only those light up in the last pane. The notes between the lines are ours: rules place them by reading the captured code.
IntroTranslate.honest.note: Fine print under the panes of the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): where the code shown comes from. {{compiler}} names the V8 version and compiler tier.

IntroHow.cpu.words.message: An emulator is as fast as the way it runs the guest's code. $t(common:product.name) interprets code that runs a few times and compiles the rest to WebAssembly. On an Apple M4, that reaches about 80% of QEMU's speed at CoreMark, from inside a browser.

IntroHow.cpu.1.words.message: The guest's code is handled a block at a time: the instructions up to the next branch, 32 at most.
IntroHow.cpu.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Guest”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.2.words.message: The first time a block runs, it is decoded into micro-ops of 8 bytes, one for each instruction. An interpreter loop runs those. Code that runs only a few times never costs a compilation.
IntroHow.cpu.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Interpreter”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.3.words.message: Every run is counted. A block that has run 1,000 times is worth compiling, and joins the next batch.
IntroHow.cpu.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Counter”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.4.words.message: The JIT emits WebAssembly for the block and its neighbors, up to 16 blocks in one function, so a loop stays inside it. The guest's registers become local variables.
IntroHow.cpu.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“JIT”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.5.words.message: The browser compiles that WebAssembly to machine code, as it does for any web page. With several cores, all of them share the same compiled code.
IntroHow.cpu.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“V8”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.words.message: WebAssembly gives a program 4 GiB of address space, and the emulator needs part of that for itself. The guest can still have 16 GiB, and nearly every access to it is a single load or store.
IntroHow.memory.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Memory” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.memory.1.words.message: A load or a store in the guest names a virtual address, as on real hardware. The guest's page tables decide what it means.
IntroHow.memory.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Address”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.2.words.message: Compiled code looks the page up in a table of recent translations: a shift, a mask, and one compare. On a hit, it adds an offset and has the real address.
IntroHow.memory.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“TLB”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.4.words.message: RAM past 3 GiB lives in more WebAssembly memories. Linux is told that each is a NUMA node without processors, so it fills them last.
IntroHow.memory.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“More memories”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.5.words.message: When the table has no answer, the instruction runs again in the interpreter. It walks the guest's page tables as a processor would, raises the fault if there is one, and fills the table for next time.
IntroHow.memory.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“Miss”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.gl.words.message: Nothing in the guest is special. Mesa's driver for virtual machines sends its commands out, and a renderer we wrote plays them on WebGL2.
IntroHow.gl.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “OpenGL” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.gl.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.gl.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.1.words.message: A program in the guest calls OpenGL or OpenGL ES, as on any Linux desktop.
IntroHow.gl.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Program”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.2.words.message: Mesa's virgl driver turns the calls into a stream of commands. It compiles shaders to an intermediate form called TGSI. $t(common:product.name)'s graphics performance and support may improve as virgl improves.
IntroHow.gl.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.3.words.message: The stream leaves through a virtio-gpu device. Textures and buffers aren't copied out: the renderer's thread reads them in the guest's memory, which is shared.
IntroHow.gl.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“virtio-gpu”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.4.words.message: Our renderer decodes the stream in a worker and translates each shader from TGSI to GLSL ES. It also does what WebGL2 can't do by itself, such as BGRA formats, base-vertex draws, and stencil per face.
IntroHow.gl.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“Renderer”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.5.words.message: Everything is drawn on one WebGL2 context, once per frame of your display. A frame from sway, the tiling Wayland compositor, costs the guest 6.6 ms this way, against 81 ms when it renders in software within the guest.
IntroHow.gl.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“WebGL2”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.video.words.message: A guest that decodes video in software would spend most of its time on it. Here the guest hands the compressed stream over, and your browser's decoder does the work.
IntroHow.video.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Video” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.video.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.video.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.1.words.message: Firefox, mpv, or GStreamer in the guest asks VA-API to decode a video, as on a PC with a hardware decoder.
IntroHow.video.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Player”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.2.words.message: Mesa's driver sends each picture's compressed data and its parameters through the same virtio-gpu device as 3D.
IntroHow.video.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.3.words.message: VA-API hands over slices and parameters, and a browser wants a stream. So the stream is put together again: H.264 with its parameter sets, AV1 with its headers, VP9 as sent.
IntroHow.video.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Bitstream”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.4.words.message: The browser's VideoDecoder decodes it, on your GPU where it can. H.264, VP9, and AV1 are offered to the guest when your browser has them. Even if your browser can only decode videos in software, that's still faster than doing it in the guest.
IntroHow.video.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“WebCodecs”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.5.words.message: The decoded picture is written into textures the guest already holds. It never passes through the guest's memory, and the guest's compositor draws it like any other surface.
IntroHow.video.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“Texture”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.vulkan.words.message: This is the deepest stack of the five. Vulkan is close to the hardware, WebGPU is not, and a real Mesa driver sits between them, compiled to WebAssembly.
IntroHow.vulkan.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Vulkan” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.vulkan.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.words.message: A program in the guest calls Vulkan: vkcube, vkQuake, the Godot editor, or a browser's own renderer.
IntroHow.vulkan.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Program”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.words.message: Mesa's Venus driver writes the Vulkan commands, nearly as they are, into rings in shared memory. No call has to stop the guest.
IntroHow.vulkan.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.words.message: On our side, virglrenderer's own Venus decoder reads the rings. It is the same C code that runs under QEMU, compiled to WebAssembly.
IntroHow.vulkan.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Decoder”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.words.message: The decoder calls a Vulkan driver we wrote on Mesa's runtime, whose hardware is WebGPU. Shaders go from SPIR-V through Mesa's NIR to WGSL, with a compiler of ours. What WebGPU lacks is emulated, such as transform feedback, multiview, and logic operations.
IntroHow.vulkan.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“Driver”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.words.message: WebGPU draws the frame. It costs 1.0 to 1.8 times what native Vulkan does on an Apple M4, and 1.9 to 3.6 times on an RTX 3070.
IntroHow.vulkan.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“WebGPU”) is the active one.

IntroRam.slider.note: Tooltip of the slider in the introduction's memory deep dive: how much RAM the guest gets.

IntroRam.value.note: The slider's value in the introduction's memory deep dive: the RAM chosen.

IntroRam.memory0.message: Memory 0 holds {{size, bytes}} of RAM (NUMA node 0) and the emulator's own 1 GiB
IntroRam.memory0.note: Over the first bar of the introduction's memory deep dive. {{size}} is the guest RAM in WebAssembly memory 0. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.spill.message: Memory {{n}} holds {{size, bytes}} of RAM (NUMA node {{n}})
IntroRam.spill.note: Over a later bar of the introduction's memory deep dive. {{n}} is the WebAssembly memory's number, which is also the NUMA node's; {{size}} its guest RAM. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.node0.message: RAM that compiled code reaches directly
IntroRam.legend.node0.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: the guest RAM in memory 0. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.spill.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: guest RAM in a later WebAssembly memory. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.own.message: The emulator's own state and heap
IntroRam.legend.own.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: the part of memory 0 the emulator keeps for itself. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.words.message: Each bar is one WebAssembly memory, 4 GiB long. Memory 0 can hold 3 GiB less 1 MiB of RAM, because the emulator keeps a gigabyte of it for decoded code and its own data. Whatever is left over goes to more memories, which Linux sees as NUMA nodes and fills last.
IntroRam.words.note: First paragraph under the bars of the introduction's memory deep dive.

IntroRam.cost.message: The other choices were measured and lost. A 64-bit WebAssembly memory cost 6% to 20% of the speed on an x86 PC, and about as much on an Apple M4. Keeping all of RAM in a second memory cost 12% to 40%. With this split, compiled code that works on node 1 takes 1.0 to 1.6 times as long as on node 0, and most machines never get there.
IntroRam.cost.note: Second paragraph under the bars of the introduction's memory deep dive: why RAM is split this way. The figures are docs/architecture.md's and docs/spill-memories.md's.

IntroGuest.caption.life.message: A third. The whole machine, kernel and programs, came with this page in one file of under 2 MB.
